headline: How one of America’s least-known senators helped pass the permitting bill
author: Theodoric Meyer

paragraphs.text: When Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt (R) appointed Alan Armstrong in March to fill a vacant Senate seat, Stitt sent him to Washington on an unusual mission: Help pass long-stalled legislation to overhaul federal permitting.
Its prospects did not look good.
Senators had spent years discussing a bill to make it easier and quicker to build power plants and transmission lines with the aim of bringing down the cost of power.

The outlines of a compromise were clear: Many Democrats supported the idea because it could help speed the transition to wind and solar power, while Republicans viewed it as a way to cut burdensome regulations. But there was widespread skepticism that Congress could strike a deal in an election year.

“Everybody was like, ‘Oh, good luck,’” Armstrong, a longtime natural gas industry executive, said in an interview. “‘We’re never going to get permitting reform done. You’re crazy if you came here for that.’”
The Senate passed the bill last week less than eight months after Armstrong’s arrival — and right before his time in the Senate is set to end.

Armstrong, a Republican, was appointed to fill the vacancy created when Trump chose Sen. Markwayne Mullin (R) as secretary of homeland security. Armstrong was barred from running for a full Senate term under state law and is set to leave the Senate on Nov. 30.

It’s not uncommon for governors to appoint a caretaker senator who does not run for a full term to fill a vacancy — but it’s rarer for such a senator to throw themselves into passing a single bill. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) described Armstrong on the Senate floor last week as probably the “most effective senator” who had served only 250 days in the chamber.

As the newest senator until the July appointment of Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina), Armstrong did not play a leading role in passing the bill. The legislation was hammered out over months by four longtime senators: Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico).
Instead, Armstrong, 64, worked obsessively to build support for passing such a bill among lawmakers and industry leaders.

The legislation is expected to accelerate the construction of a wide variety of infrastructure — including roads, housing and energy projects — if it becomes law. It has the support of fossil fuel and renewable energy interests but has drawn opposition from some Democrats and environmental groups that argue it makes it harder to stop oil and gas projects.

Armstrong estimated he spent more than 90 percent of time in the Senate working on permitting. His fellow Republican senators grew tired of hearing him talk about the bill again and again during their weekly closed-door lunches, he said.

“He was kind of Johnny-one-note,” Capito said. “I mean, that’s all he talked about. And that actually was helpful, because it kept [the spotlight on the issue] while we were negotiating maybe a little more subtly.”

Stitt said he appointed Armstrong after conferring with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) due to Armstrong’s expertise in the permitting process. Armstrong was deeply versed on the issue as a former chief executive of Williams, a natural gas pipeline company — but he knew little about the arcane rules and traditions of the Senate.
Armstrong said he was shocked by the Senate’s “vote-a-rama” tradition, in which senators spend hours voting on amendments late into the night.

“You get all these well-educated, accomplished people to sit around way past their bedtimes until 4 in the morning to really accomplish something that they already knew at 6 o’clock in the evening the night before,” Armstrong said. “And it’s just to grandstand, and it’s just to make a TV recording.”
The permitting bill won the support of almost every Senate Republican but divided Democrats. Some Democrats raised concerns that it would hurt Native American tribes and damage the environment.
The bill has yet to pass the House, and some Democrats have advocated opposing it and writing their own bill once the party regains control of Congress in January.

“We can make it easier to build good things without selling out our friends and neighbors,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-Massachusetts) said in a statement. “Let’s do that in January with a Democratic majority writing the bill, not fossil fuel companies and their lobbyists.”

Others Democrats have warned that waiting would torpedo the bill. Heinrich wrote Monday that “there is no alternative — this year or next — that can become law” because it would need some Republican support in the Senate and Trump’s signature.

One of the 14 Democrats who supported the bill in the Senate was Sen. John Hickenlooper (Colorado), who first met Armstrong when he was an energy executive and Hickenlooper was governor of Colorado. They ran into each other on the Senate floor soon after Armstrong arrived, and Hickenlooper offered to let Armstrong live in the basement apartment of his Capitol Hill rowhouse during his tenure in Washington.
In lieu of rent, Armstrong agreed to supply food and wine for bipartisan dinners that Hickenlooper hosts for senators to discuss tough policy problems — including how to overhaul permitting.
“His value has been to keep pushing,” Hickenlooper said of Armstrong’s role in passing the bill. “He’s got a sense of urgency that’s been unusual for this building.”

Armstrong’s conviction that the United States needed to overhaul its permitting rules was shaped by his years running Williams. In 2016, for instance, New York state blocked construction of the company’s Constitution natural gas pipeline, citing water-quality concerns. The project would’ve moved forward if the permitting bill had been law, Armstrong said.
Still, Armstrong said the bill, if it becomes law, is likely to help Williams in some ways but hurt it in others by making it easier for competitors to build pipelines.

“When you’re the incumbent and nobody else can build anything, your pricing power gets to be pretty outsized,” Armstrong said. “And that’s great for the company in the short term. In the long term, that’s terrible for our country and it’s terrible for our ability to provide low-cost energy, which ultimately is what’s going to keep a company like Williams in business.”

Armstong’s successor, Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma), is set to be sworn in next week after winning the race for a full Senate term. Despite his frustrations with aspects of the Senate, Armstrong said he has more hope for the institution now than when he was appointed.

“I arrived in Washington believing that America’s permitting problems could be fixed,” Armstrong said last week in a speech on the Senate floor. “I leave with a much broader conviction: that many of our country’s greatest challenges are within our ability to solve if we are willing to do the very hard work of finding common ground for the benefit of our nation.”
